meta.title: Deploying Neural Networks on FPGAs for Earth Observation satellites
meta.authorsHtml: Georgios Flengas<sup>∗</sup><sup>1</sup>, Nicolò Ghielmetti<sup>1</sup>, Robert Bayer<sup>2</sup>, Sioni Summers<sup>1</sup>

meta.venue: Proceedings of the 3rd Conference on AI in and for Space (SPAICE 2026)

abstract: Following advances in technology and reduction in cost, availability of data onboard satellites has been increasing. Machine Learning has been shown to be effective at identifying relevant data for downlink, but needs to be optimised in order to be deployed onboard within a limited compute and power envelope. We present developments to deploy neural networks for image segmentation onto FPGA SoC processors. Our inference engines are based on the hls4ml and CGRA4ML software, which we have extended to target NanoXplore NG-ULTRA devices. We showcase our developments on the task of identifying plastics pollution in the oceans.

blocks.html: The importance of onboard ML processing for satellites grows as the industry gathers pace, reflecting the lower cost of launching small satellites and the greater fidelity and data volume produced by sensors. ML can be used onboard to identify objects of importance in Earth Observation images, and selectively send only relevant data, avoiding unnecessary data transmission to the ground. In scenarios like disaster detection, for example, of forest fires [1], ML can be used to detect events in real time and send ‘beacons’ or alerts with a rapid response time.

Several technological challenges present an obstacle to more widespread deployment of ML onboard satellites. Datacentre GPUs are off-limits due to tight space and power budgets. Instead, low-power edge devices are preferred, requiring smaller neural networks and efficient hardware utilization. Electronics operating on satellites are also subjected to a harsh radiation environment, requiring use of specialist technologies. FPGAs, which we target for this work, have been shown to address some of these challenges [2].

We demonstrate deployment on FPGA SoC devices using hls4ml [3] and CGRA4ML [4] to bring efficient ML compute to the Earth Observation setting. These two approaches target alternative pathways to FPGA ML inference: hls4ml is a dataflow architecture that produces fast, efficient gateware for a specific Neural Network; CGRA4ML is a more general purpose ML accelerator and compiler that creates a processing array for a given neural network. The focus of hls4ml is on compute efficiency at the expense of hardware footprint, while CGRA4ML provides scalability to larger neural networks.

We have carried out additional development on FPGA SoC fast inference software, especially targeting imagesegmentation neural networks to be deployed on NanoXplore devices. These European FPGA SoCs are radiationtolerant devices targeted for space applications. Our contributions include further optimisation of streaming U-Net implementations for more demanding image-segmentation workloads, development of a new hls4ml backend and deployment flow for NanoXplore devices using PandA- Bambu, and the porting of CGRA4ML to the NanoXplore NG-ULTRA platform.

We showcase our developments on the task of identifying plastics pollution in the oceans. We demonstrate enhancements toward deployment of U-Net segmentation models for this application on the NanoXplore NG-ULTRA, establishing novel deployment paths based of hls4ml and CGRA4ML. We also target AMD/Xilinx devices to develop and evaluate our hls4ml optimisations against an established benchmark.

The methodology is described in Section 2. Our developments targeting streaming U-Nets, PandA-Bambu, and CGRA4ML are described in Sections 2.3.2 to 2.3.4, respectively, with results from in-hardware deployments presented in Section 3.

In order to demonstrate our developments on improved capabilities for ML deployment on FPGAs, we showcase the end-to-end workflow from model training to measuring the performance on an FPGA device. We targeted neural networks suitable for image data, aligned with the Earth Observation use case. We focussed more specifically on the U-Net model architecture for image segmentation - identifying the category of each pixel of an image. As the neural network inference architectures considered in this work rely on matrix-vector multiplication as the core compute primitive, we additionally showcase results using multi-layer perceptrons, and classification-type convolutional neural networks without the upscaling performed by U-Net.

blocks.html: We have used four representative datasets to carry out the studies in this work: jet tagging [5]; MNIST handwritten digits; cloud segmentation (ALCD) [6], and the Marine Debris and Oil Spill (MADOS) dataset for plastics pollution [7]. Table 1 describes the modality and size of each of the datasets used in this study.

The jet tagging dataset is an open dataset from the particle physics community, summarising particle jets using 16 high-level features (tabular), with a task of classifying the type of particle from five different classes. ALCD comprises 38 scenes of Sentinel-2 image data, captured between 2017- 2018, with 8 classes of different cloud types and common backgrounds. MADOS is an open dataset targeting identification of plastics pollution in the oceans. The dataset comprises 174 scenes of Sentinel-2 image data, totalling 2803 patches of 240×240 pixels. Images were captured between 2015-2022, covering 22 countries focussed on coastal regions. Per-pixel labels have been provided through hand annotation, labelling 16 classes focussed on plastics pollution (marine debris) and objects commonly misidentified as plastics pollution.

We use MLPs and convolutional neural networks for the classification benchmarks, while focusing on the U-Net architecture for image segmentation [8]. This model architecture, depicted in Figure 1, compresses the image down to a latent space before expanding again to the original dimensions, propagating the higher-resolution data forward using skip connections. Models of the similar ENet architecture with 10k parameters [9], and sparse U-Net models up to 50k parameters trained on ALCD [10], have previously been deployed on FPGAs with hls4ml.

Quantization is a key enabler of more efficient ML inference. ML models are known to be robust against even extreme quantization. For ultimate performance down to very low bit representations, Quantization Aware Training is preferred. When targeting a dataflow architecture, as with hls4ml, where each NN layer uses discrete FPGA logic, model parameters may have heterogeneous quantization. That is, the weights, biases, and activations of each layer may use different quantization. We have used and contributed to the QONNX tool for representation of heterogeneously quantized neural networks.

blocks.html: FPGAs provide a blank template on which to map a specific computational design. Tailoring of the design to the FPGA fabric is needed to achieve high performance. When it comes to deployment of ML on FPGAs, two common approaches are: model-specific dataflow architectures; and configurable data processing units. Heterogeneous hardware/software architectures provide another design point by partitioning computation between the CPU and reusable accelerator logic in the FPGA fabric.

2.3.1 hls4ml on Xilinx devices hls4ml [3] is a tool for producing dataflow implementations of neural networks on FPGAs. The tool provides optimized HLS implementations of neural network inference components, and a software infrastructure to map a user-provided model onto those components. As a dataflow architecture, each NN layer is mapped onto different logic resources in the FPGA. For streaming data, as used here, FIFOs are placed in between NN layers to orchestrate the movement of data along the pipeline.

Established hls4ml deployments target AMD and Xilinx FPGAs, for which there is prior support. We use a ZCU102 kit from AMD, which hosts a Zynq UltraScale+ XCZU9EG SoC and provides resources representative of those available onboard CubeSats. Several enhancements to the AMD/Xilinx support in hls4ml were developed in order to carry out this work. Notably, improvements to FIFO sizing and balancing the latency of modules in the dataflow pipeline were essential to increase the deployable model size from 50k to 100k parameters for ALCD. This established flow provides the basis for the additional optimisations required by the more demanding MADOS U-Net described in Section 2.3.2.

In order to benchmark the performance, we have also deployed the same U-Net models on the ZCU102 kit using Vitis AI [11]. Vitis AI is a DPU ML accelerator and associated runtime software from AMD, representing a popular commercial solution. Compared to hls4ml, the DPU is a reconfigurable accelerator which implements generic ML inference components and maps a specific ML model onto instructions that are executed on the accelerator.

Previous Edge SpAIce work deployed a 50k-parameter ALCD U-Net on the ZCU102 [10], enabled by FIFO-depth optimisation that removed an earlier BRAM bottleneck, while subsequent project developments reported ALCD U-Net deployments with approximately 100k parameters. MADOS presents a more demanding workload, with 240 × 240 × 5 inputs and 16 logits per pixel, reduced to 10 evaluation classes in software. Retaining a fully streaming implementation therefore required further hls4ml optimisation.

A key development was an operations-aware parallelisation strategy for the streaming dataflow design. Since pipeline throughput is determined by its slowest stage, additional parallelism in faster layers consumes resources without improving overall throughput. We estimate the workload of each convolution and assign a layer-specific parallelisation (reuse factor), to target a common pipeline service rate. Lower-workload layers are therefore serialised more aggressively, reducing unnecessary parallelism and buffering from producer-consumer rate mismatches.

Further savings were obtained by fusing the repeated depthwise-separable convolution (SepConv) pattern. In the standard streaming implementation, padding, depth-wise convolution, and pointwise convolution form separate dataflow stages connected by intermediate streams. Our custom SepConv kernel combines these operations into a single block and retains depthwise results locally for direct pointwise consumption, avoiding materialisation of the intermediate feature map and its associated stream boundary. Since this pattern occurs 20 times in the evaluated U-Net, the savings accumulate across the complete design.
We evaluate these optimisations on a distilled 10kparameter MADOS U-Net that fits and meets timing on the ZCU102; results are presented in Section 3.

hls4ml relies on an HLS compiler to translate its generated C++ into synthesizable RTL. While its established backends target tools such as Vitis HLS, the NanoXplore ecosystem does not provide an equivalent HLS compiler. We therefore use PandA-Bambu [12], an open-source HLS framework capable of targeting both Xilinx and NanoXplore FPGAs. Xilinx devices provide an established platform for validating and benchmarking the new backend against existing hls4ml flows, while NanoXplore NG-ULTRA is the target platform for extending hls4ml deployment to European radiation-tolerant FPGA SoCs.

In collaboration with the PandA developers at Politecnico di Milano, we developed a new hls4ml backend for Bambu. The backend provides Bambu-specific code generation, datatypes, compiler directives and numerical templates, and supports both parallel and streaming I/O. In parallel, Bambu itself has been extended with features required by hls4ml, including array partitioning, dataflow execution and streaming-channel support. Operator coverage remains under active development, particularly for the more complex layers required by U-Net architectures.

Building on this backend, we developed a complete NG-ULTRA deployment flow. The Bambu-generated core is wrapped with the required AXI4 interfaces and clocking, while a clean interface separates the open hls4ml flow from the proprietary NanoXplore place-and-route and bitstream-generation tools. The resulting path has been validated end to end on NG-ULTRA with both parallel and streaming hls4ml designs, from model conversion and HLS synthesis through bitstream generation and hardware inference. This establishes a complete hls4ml deployment path for NanoXplore devices and provides the foundation for extending the flow towards U-Net models.

CGRA4ML [4] addresses the resource scaling of spatially instantiated dataflow inference. Whereas hls4ml implements each layer using dedicated logic, CGRA4ML reuses a configurable Processing Element (PE) array for convolution and dense operations. A CPU orchestrates execution, data transfers, and lightweight or irregular operations. The frontend partitions the model into ‘bundles’ and generates their runtime configuration and execution schedule. This decouples FPGA resource use from network depth and enables larger architectures such as ResNet-50 and PointNet.

We ported this architecture to NanoXplore NG-ULTRA while preserving the PE array and bundle abstraction. The RTL was adapted to the SystemVerilog subset supported by Impulse, and a reusable VHDL shell integrates the accelerator with the SoC clock, reset, memory, and control interfaces. An LLPP-to-AXI-Lite bridge maps the Cortex- R52 control window to the accelerator address space. We aggregate layer activation reads and writes into one interface, keeping weight reads on a second interface, to fit within the two interfaces available on the NG-ULTRA.

Because the original CGRA4ML software was written for Zynq, we developed a bare-metal runtime for the NG- ULTRA Cortex-R52. It manages data movement, cache handling, accelerator control, and CPU-side operations such as activation, pooling, residual connections, dense layers, softmax, and data repacking. Host-side tools prepare the runtime configuration and reference outputs used for numerical validation.

During hardware validation, accelerator outputs were compared against host-generated references after every bundle and after CPU-side residual, dense, and softmax stages. End-to-end execution time was measured from application startup to the final softmax output, including initialization, cache maintenance, data movement, accelerator execution, and CPU post-processing.

The resulting NG-ULTRA flow was validated end-to-end on hardware using a multi-bundle ResNet-style network. CPU-side nearest-neighbour upsampling has also been implemented and validated as part of extending the flow toward U-Net-style architectures. Implementation and execution results are presented in Section 3.

The implementations evaluated in this work are summarized in Table 2. We present results for each of the methodologies described in Sections 2.3. For each development, we deploy the model closest to a large U-Net segmentation model trained on the MADOS dataset that can currently be achieved. We use other models, either smaller or using a different NN architecture where necessary due to either resource constraints or feature completeness.

On the established ZCU102 flow, the approximately 100kparameter ALCD U-Net reaches 1,500 FPS at 3.7 W with hls4ml, compared with 40 FPS at 9.4 W using Vitis AI, corresponding to a 24-fold improvement in pixel throughput per Watt. For the MADOS dataset, the developments described in 2.3.2 enabled the first deployment of a model on ZCU102 with hls4ml. Together, these developments produced a factor 2 reduction in the Block RAM (BRAM) usage, which were essential to fitting the 9.9k parameters model within available resource contsraints and to achieving timing closure.

Figure 2 shows example MADOS images segmented by the QONNX model together with the corresponding hls4ml CPU-emulated and ZCU102 in-hardware predictions. The CPU implementation closely reproduces the QONNX output, with 99.998% post-processed pixel agreement, while the deployed hardware reaches 97.85% agreement. The residual hardware-level discrepancy is under investigation; nevertheless, the results demonstrate successful end-to-end execution of the MADOS streaming dataflow model on the ZCU102.

PandA-Bambu is evaluated both as an open-source HLS backend and as the basis of the new NanoXplore deployment path. On the representative Jet-MLP benchmark targeting the Xilinx xc7z020 part, PandA-Bambu produces a substantially smaller implementation than Vitis HLS, at the cost of increased latency. A separate 71-parameter MLP was used as an integration demonstrator on NG-ULTRA, completing synthesis, place-and-route, bitstream generation, and on-board inference using both io_parallel and io_stream interfaces. This validates the complete hls4ml-to-NanoXplore deployment path while support for the additional layer operators required by U-Net remains under development.

We validate our port using a seven-bundle, 12,742-parameter ResNet-style classifier trained on the MNIST dataset, occupying 17.58% of the available fabric elements and 7.44% of the memory blocks with no DSP usage. With a 40 MHz target clock for the FPGA fabric, the complete application achieves a mean end-to-end latency of 7.147 ms, including initialization, cache maintenance, DDR/OCM transfers, accelerator execution, CPU-side inter-bundle processing, and softmax. All accelerator bundles and intermediate CPU-side stages were numerically validated on hardware. While we will continue to develop features required to target segmentation models like U-Net, this deployment of a ResNet architecture on NG-ULTRA represents a significant step towards deployment of ML in future Earth Observation missions based on NanoXplore devices.

We have presented developments toward deploying imagesegmentation networks trained on the MADOS dataset on FPGAs for onboard detection of marine pollution. By extending hls4ml, we improved support for larger streaming U-Nets on AMD devices and demonstrated their performance against Vitis AI. We also established two complementary paths to deploying ML inference on NanoXplore NG-ULTRA: a new hls4ml backend based on PandA- Bambu, and a port of CGRA4ML with a custom runtime.

Our results present a significant step towards utilisation and integration of ML inference on NanoXplore devices. We have developed both dataflow and processing element based inference engines. Future work will focus on completing the feature set required to deploy large U- Net models, trained on the MADOS dataset, targeting the NG-ULTRA. Both of these developments are based on open source compiler chains, and will form part of the broader Fast Machine Learning software ecosystem, making them accessible to the wider community.
